gloss_readable: This term refers to the outer surface of the human body—the skin or flesh as a physical covering. In Acts 19:12, handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched Paul's skin were taken to the sick, and diseases left them. The multilingual evidence (English 'skin', Spanish 'cuerpo', French 'peau') confirms this physical, tactile sense of bodily surface contact, emphasizing the concrete, material nature of the healing objects.

senses.1: The outer covering of the human body, the skin or surface flesh. Used in Acts 19:12 where Paul's personal items absorb healing power through direct contact with his bodily surface, illustrating early Christian belief in tactile transmission of divine power through physical proximity.

gloss_readable: A specific wind from the northwest direction, known in Latin as Corus. In Acts 27:12, this wind is referenced in the description of a harbor that opens toward the southwest and northwest. The consistency across translations (English 'northwest', Spanish 'noroeste', French 'nord-ouest') reflects precise nautical terminology important to Luke's detailed account of Paul's perilous sea journey to Rome.

senses.1: The northwest wind, a precise meteorological term used in ancient Mediterranean navigation. Acts 27:12 employs this technical vocabulary to describe the orientation of Fair Havens harbor in Crete, showing Luke's attention to authentic seafaring detail in Paul's voyage narrative.

gloss_terse: false apostle, fraudulent messenger claiming apostolic authority
gloss_readable: A compound term describing someone who falsely claims to be an apostle—a deceptive religious figure who assumes apostolic authority without genuine divine commission. Paul uses this sharp designation in 2 Corinthians 11:13 to denounce opponents in Corinth who masqueraded as Christ's emissaries. The multilingual glosses (English 'false-apostles', Spanish 'falsos-apóstoles', French 'faux-apôtre') preserve the compound structure, emphasizing both the counterfeit nature and the specific office being falsely claimed.

senses.1: One who fraudulently presents themselves as an apostle of Christ. In 2 Corinthians 11:13, Paul unmasks such figures as 'deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ,' warning the Corinthian church against accepting unauthorized teachers who exploit apostolic credibility for their own gain.

gloss_terse: false teacher, one who teaches error or heresy
gloss_readable: Someone who propagates false doctrine or heretical teaching within the community of faith. Peter warns in 2 Peter 2:1 that such false teachers will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them. The term appears across languages as a compound construction (Spanish 'falsos-maestros', English 'false-teachers'), highlighting both the pedagogical role and its corruption, a critical concern in early Christianity's battle against doctrinal distortion.

senses.1: A teacher who leads others astray with erroneous doctrine. Used in 2 Peter 2:1 within a prophetic warning about infiltrators who will covertly bring in damaging teachings, paralleling the false prophets of Israel's past but now threatening the New Covenant community with theological deception.

gloss_readable: Persons who habitually speak lies or engage in deliberate falsehood. In 1 Timothy 4:2, Paul describes false teachers whose consciences are seared as 'speaking lies in hypocrisy'—the genitive construction emphasizes their fundamental character as liars. The consistent rendering across languages (Spanish 'de-mentirosos', English 'of-liars', German 'Luegner') captures this attribution of moral character, identifying lying as a defining trait of those who oppose sound doctrine.

senses.1: Those characterized by speaking falsehood, especially in religious contexts. The term appears in 1 Timothy 4:2 describing the hypocritical nature of false teachers whose teaching comes 'through the hypocrisy of liars,' indicating that mendacity is not incidental but essential to their corrupting influence in the church.

gloss_terse: falsely named, bearing a name that misrepresents reality
gloss_readable: Something incorrectly or deceptively labeled, bearing a designation that doesn't match its true nature. Paul uses this adjective in 1 Timothy 6:20 to warn Timothy against 'what is falsely called knowledge'—presumably Gnostic claims to superior spiritual insight. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'falsamente-llamado', English 'falsely-named', French 'faux-nommé') consistently captures the gap between the claimed identity and actual reality, a crucial apologetic distinction.

senses.1: Wrongly designated or bearing a false title. In 1 Timothy 6:20, Paul warns against 'the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge,' critiquing teachings that claim intellectual or spiritual superiority but actually oppose the truth of the gospel. The term exposes pretentious claims as hollow.

gloss_readable: A deliberate falsehood or untruth, distinct from mere error. In Romans 3:7, Paul poses a rhetorical question about whether God's truthfulness is enhanced by human lies—if divine truth becomes more evident through contrast with our falsehood. The translations (Spanish 'mentira', French 'mensonge', English 'lie', German 'Luege') consistently point to intentional deception, not accidental mistake, underscoring the moral dimension of speaking what contradicts reality.

senses.1: An intentional falsehood or deceitful statement. Used in Romans 3:7 within Paul's diatribe addressing objections to his gospel: 'But if through my lie the truth of God abounded to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner?' The term emphasizes human mendacity as a foil to divine truthfulness.

gloss_readable: Secret communication, especially gossip or slander spoken in hushed tones. Paul lists this vice in 2 Corinthians 12:20 among the relational sins he fears finding in Corinth—quarreling, jealousy, anger, and 'whisperings' that undermine community. The multilingual glosses (Spanish 'murmuraciones', French 'murmure', English 'gossip', German 'Gefluster') capture both the quiet manner of speaking and its destructive content, highlighting how covert speech damages fellowship.

senses.1: Secretive gossip or slanderous talk spoken in low tones. In 2 Corinthians 12:20, Paul includes 'whisperings' in a catalog of divisive behaviors that fracture Christian community, suggesting that this form of communication—characterized by secrecy and malicious intent—is as harmful as open conflict.

gloss_terse: whisperers, those who spread secret slander or gossip
gloss_readable: People who engage in covert slander or gossip, speaking malicious things in secret. Paul condemns such individuals in Romans 1:29 within his comprehensive indictment of pagan society, listing 'whisperers' alongside other moral failures. The term across languages (Spanish 'murmuradores', French 'calomniateur', English 'gossips', German 'Verleumder') consistently identifies those who damage reputations through secretive, malicious speech rather than open confrontation.

senses.1: Those who practice covert slander or malicious gossip. Romans 1:29 includes 'whisperers' in Paul's dark portrait of humanity apart from God, identifying them as people who undermine others through secretive accusation and rumor-spreading, reflecting the social fragmentation that results from rejecting divine truth.

gloss_terse: grow cold, lose warmth or fervor
gloss_readable: To become cold, lose warmth—used metaphorically of diminishing love or spiritual fervor. Jesus warns in Matthew 24:12 that because lawlessness will increase, 'the love of many will grow cold.' The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'se-enfriará', French 'se-refroidir', English 'will-grow-cold') uniformly employs temperature metaphors to describe the cooling of affection and devotion, a vivid image of spiritual decline amid mounting evil and persecution.

senses.1: To lose warmth, become cold—metaphorically of love or devotion fading. In Matthew 24:12, Jesus prophesies that escalating wickedness in the end times will cause many believers' love to 'grow cold,' describing spiritual apathy and relational breakdown as consequences of intensified evil. The passive form suggests external pressure causing internal cooling.

gloss_readable: To rub or crumble something between the hands, particularly grain heads. In Luke 6:1, the disciples are described as picking heads of grain and 'rubbing them in their hands' to separate kernels from chaff—an action that provoked Pharisaic criticism as Sabbath work. The consistent translations (Spanish 'frotando', French 'frotter', English 'rubbing') capture this tactile agricultural action, central to the controversy over what constitutes forbidden Sabbath labor.

senses.1: To rub or crumble grain heads between the hands to extract kernels. Luke 6:1 depicts disciples 'rubbing' grain on the Sabbath, an action the Pharisees condemned as unlawful threshing. This agricultural detail becomes theologically significant in Jesus's defense of Sabbath freedom over rigid legalism.

gloss_readable: To purchase or acquire something through payment. In Acts 7:16, Stephen recounts how Abraham bought a tomb from the sons of Hamor at Shechem for a sum of silver. The term across languages (Spanish 'compró', French 'acheter', English 'bought') consistently denotes commercial transaction and property acquisition, an important detail in tracing the patriarchal connection to the promised land through purchased burial rights.

senses.1: To acquire through purchase or financial transaction. Acts 7:16 uses this verb to describe Abraham's acquisition of a burial plot, though the exact historical details are debated. The commercial nature of the transaction establishes legal ownership and permanent connection to the land, anticipating Israel's future inheritance.

gloss_readable: A bird's egg, typically a hen's egg in domestic contexts. Jesus uses this common food item in Luke 11:12 within a rhetorical question about parental provision: if a child asks for an egg, what father would give a scorpion? The multilingual glosses (Spanish 'un-huevo', French 'œuf', English 'an-egg') uniformly identify this ordinary food, which Jesus employs to illustrate the reliability of divine provision compared to human parental instincts.

senses.1: An egg, particularly a hen's egg as food. In Luke 11:12, Jesus invokes the egg as an example of a normal, harmless food a child might request, contrasting it with a scorpion—something harmful that no good father would substitute. The image reinforces trust in God's benevolent provision.

gloss_readable: To roar or howl, especially of predatory animals like lions. Peter warns in 1 Peter 5:8 that 'your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.' The participle form across languages (Spanish 'rugiente', French 'rugissant', English 'roaring') captures the terrifying sound of a hunting predator, making the devil's threat visceral and immediate—not abstract but dangerous and actively seeking prey.

senses.1: To roar like a lion or other predator, expressing threat and aggression. In 1 Peter 5:8, the devil is depicted as 'a roaring lion' prowling for victims. The auditory imagery intensifies the warning: Satan's approach is not silent but announces his predatory intent, demanding vigilance and resistance from believers.

gloss_readable: The prophet Hosea, whose ministry to the northern kingdom of Israel emphasized God's covenant love despite Israel's unfaithfulness. Paul quotes from Hosea in Romans 9:25, citing the prophet's message that God would call those 'not my people' to become 'my people'—a text Paul applies to the inclusion of Gentiles in God's redemptive plan. The name appears consistently across translations as a proper noun identifying this eighth-century prophet.

senses.1: The prophet Hosea, author of the book bearing his name. Romans 9:25 cites Hosea's prophecy about God's mercy extending beyond ethnic Israel, using the prophet's marriage metaphor to illustrate divine grace reclaiming the unfaithful. Paul reads Hosea's oracle as foreshadowing Gentile inclusion in the covenant community.

gloss_terse: as if, as it were, like
gloss_readable: A comparative particle meaning 'as if' or 'as it were,' introducing hypothetical or approximate comparisons. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 15:8 to describe his encounter with the risen Christ: 'Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.' The term across languages (Spanish 'como-si', French 'comme-si', German 'gleichsam', English 'as-if') signals that Paul's apostolic calling was abnormal—like a premature birth, outside the natural sequence of apostolic appointments.

senses.1: Comparative particle introducing a hypothetical or approximate comparison, 'as if' or 'as it were.' In 1 Corinthians 15:8, Paul describes himself 'as to one untimely born,' using this particle to acknowledge the exceptional, even unnatural character of his Damascus road encounter compared to the other apostles' post-resurrection experiences.

gloss_readable: A Persian name belonging to one of the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus. In Esther 1:10, Abagtha is among the chamberlains commanded to bring Queen Vashti before the king at his banquet. The name reflects Persian court culture and administration, with multilingual glosses preserving the proper noun across translations. The 'and' prefix in Hebrew indicates this name appears within a list of officials.

senses.1: A eunuch in the court of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I of Persia). Esther 1:10 names Abagtha among seven chamberlains ordered to escort Queen Vashti to the king's feast—a command she famously refuses, setting in motion the events that elevate Esther to the throne.

gloss_readable: Complete destruction or annihilation, especially in contexts of warfare and violence. Esther 9:5 describes the Jews striking their enemies 'with the sword, killing and destroying them, and doing as they pleased to those who hated them.' The term appears in phrases emphasizing total military defeat. The multilingual glosses (Spanish 'y-destrucción', English 'and-destruction') consistently render this as comprehensive ruin, not mere defeat.

senses.1: Total destruction or annihilation in warfare. In Esther 9:5, the term appears in a triad 'stroke of the sword, killing, and destruction,' emphasizing the thoroughness of Jewish victory over their enemies on the appointed day. The word intensifies beyond simple military defeat to complete obliteration.

gloss_readable: Destruction or ruin, appearing in construct relationship with other nouns. In Esther 8:6, Esther pleads with the king: 'How can I endure to see the disaster that would come to my people? Or how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred?' The construct form 'in-destruction-of' links the abstract concept to the concrete victims—Esther's people. The emotional weight of this rhetorical question drives her urgent appeal to reverse Haman's decree.

senses.1: Destruction in construct relationship, 'destruction of' someone or something. Esther 8:6 uses this form in Esther's passionate plea before Ahasuerus, asking how she could bear to witness 'the destruction of my kindred.' The construct grammatically binds the abstract calamity to her specific, beloved people.

gloss_terse: my father (vocative or possessive), O my father
gloss_readable: A term meaning 'my father,' used either as a vocative address or possessive designation. Job 34:36 is textually complex, with this form possibly functioning as an interjection ('O my father') or as part of the verb 'I entreat.' The BDB suggests it may be a dialectical form expressing entreaty: 'Would that Job were tried!' The multilingual evidence shows interpretive variation, with some treating it as kinship language and others as an expression of wish or prayer.

senses.1: Possibly 'my father' as vocative or part of an entreaty expression. Job 34:36 presents textual challenges, with this form potentially expressing Elihu's wish or prayer that Job be thoroughly tested. The uncertainty reflects the verse's grammatical difficulty, though the kinship term may carry overtones of appeal or invocation.

gloss_terse: reed, papyrus, water plant used for boats
gloss_readable: A reed or papyrus plant, particularly one used in constructing lightweight, swift boats. Job 9:26 speaks of days passing 'like reed boats, like an eagle swooping on its prey'—images of speed and transience. The parallel passage in Isaiah 18:2 refers to 'vessels of papyrus,' indicating watercraft made from bundled reeds. These boats, known from ancient Egypt, were remarkably fast despite their fragile appearance.

senses.1: Reed or papyrus used to construct boats. In Job 9:26, Job laments the swift passage of his days, comparing them to 'reed boats'—lightweight papyrus craft known for their speed. The image captures both velocity and fragility, reflecting Job's sense that life rushes past without pause or substance.

gloss_readable: An exclamation expressing pain, sorrow, or distress—similar to 'alas!' or 'woe!' In Proverbs 23:29, this term appears in parallel with 'woe' in a rhetorical question: 'Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife?' The verse introduces a warning against excessive drinking. The interjection gives voice to the suffering and regret that follow drunkenness, personifying the consequences of indulgence as cries of anguish.

senses.1: An exclamation of pain, sorrow, or regret. Proverbs 23:29 uses this interjection in a series of rhetorical questions identifying the drunkard as one who experiences 'woe' and 'sorrow.' The parallel structure intensifies the emotional landscape of alcohol abuse, moving from external conflict to internal anguish.

gloss_readable: A term possibly meaning 'slaughter' or 'carnage,' though its authenticity is disputed. It appears in Ezekiel 21:15 (Hebrew 21:20) in the phrase 'slaughter of the sword,' describing the weapon's deadly purpose. Many scholars, including the lexicon itself, suggest this may be a textual error for a more common word for slaughter. The translations vary, with some preserving the term and others emending it.

senses.1: Slaughter or carnage, though possibly a scribal error. Ezekiel 21:15 describes a sword appointed 'for slaughter,' emphasizing the blade's deadly intent in God's judgment against Jerusalem. Whether original or corrupt, the term functions within the passage's violent imagery of divine wrath executed through Babylonian invasion.

gloss_readable: Watermelons or other melons, a fruit the Israelites remembered from Egypt. In Numbers 11:5, the people complain in the wilderness, nostalgically recalling the foods they ate freely in Egypt: 'We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic.' This list represents the variety and abundance they associate with their former captivity, now idealized in contrast to manna's monotony.

senses.1: Watermelons or similar melons from Egypt. Numbers 11:5 includes 'the melons' in the Israelites' nostalgic catalog of Egyptian foods, reflecting their selective memory that romanticizes slavery's diet while forgetting its oppression. The fruit symbolizes perceived abundance lost, fueling their discontent in the desert.

gloss_readable: The personal name of King Hezekiah's mother, called Abi in 2 Kings 18:2 and Abijah elsewhere. She was the daughter of Zechariah. The name means 'Yahweh is my father' and appears in various forms across the biblical text. In Chronicles, the fuller form Abijah is used, while Kings employs the shortened Abi. Her mention follows the pattern of identifying the queen mother in Judean royal records.

senses.1: The mother of King Hezekiah, daughter of Zechariah. 2 Kings 18:2 records that Hezekiah was twenty-five when he began to reign, and his mother's name was Abi. Her identification follows the Deuteronomistic pattern of naming the king's mother, suggesting the queen mother's significant status in Judean monarchy.

gloss_readable: A personal name meaning 'my father has gathered,' belonging to a descendant of Korah from the tribe of Levi. Exodus 6:24 lists Abiasaph among the sons of Korah, establishing his place in the Levitical genealogy. The name also appears as Ebiasaph in Chronicles. This figure is part of the Korahite line that survived Korah's rebellion and became an important Levitical family serving in temple worship.

senses.1: A Levite, son (or descendant) of Korah. Exodus 6:24 names Abiasaph in the genealogy tracing the priestly line through Levi. Despite his ancestor Korah's rebellion and destruction, Abiasaph's line continued and eventually served as temple singers and gatekeepers, showing God's mercy extending beyond one generation's sin.

gloss_readable: A personal name meaning 'my father is majesty,' belonging to a Benjamite in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants. First Chronicles 8:3 identifies Abihud as one of the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. The name, combining 'father' with 'majesty' or 'splendor,' reflects the theophoric naming pattern common in Israelite culture, attributing glory to God as father. The Benjamite genealogies preserve tribal identity during and after exile.

senses.1: A Benjamite, son of Bela. 1 Chronicles 8:3 lists Abihud among the sons of Bela, who was Benjamin's firstborn. This genealogical notice preserves the internal structure of Benjamin's tribe, important for maintaining tribal identity and land claims after the exile. The name's meaning ('my father is majesty') reflects piety toward God.

gloss_terse: caper berry, fruit used as aphrodisiac or stimulant
gloss_readable: The caper berry, a small fruit from the caper plant (Capparis spinosa), believed to stimulate appetite or desire. Ecclesiastes 12:5 uses this image in a poetic description of old age: 'the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and the caper berry fails.' If the caper was valued as a stimulant or aphrodisiac, its failure symbolizes the loss of vitality and desire in advanced age, completing the chapter's vivid allegory of bodily decline.

senses.1: The caper berry or caper-bud, possibly valued as an appetite or desire stimulant. In Ecclesiastes 12:5, 'the caper berry fails' within an extended metaphor of aging and death. Its failure likely represents the loss of appetite, vitality, or sexual desire—another sign that the body's systems are shutting down before death.

gloss_readable: A personal name meaning 'my father is goodness,' belonging to a Benjamite listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. The name appears in 1 Chronicles 8:11 as one of the sons of Shaharaim by his wife Hushim. Like many names in the Chronicler's Benjamite genealogy, it combines a familial term ('father') with a divine attribute ('goodness'), expressing faith in God's benevolent character.

senses.1: A Benjamite, son of Shaharaim. 1 Chronicles 8:11 names Abitub among Shaharaim's children born in Moab, part of the detailed Benjamite genealogies that trace family lines through exile and return. The name ('my father is goodness') testifies to parental faith in God's good character despite uncertain circumstances.

gloss_terse: roll up, coil, twist upward (of smoke)
gloss_readable: To roll up, twist, or coil—particularly used of smoke rising and billowing. Isaiah 9:18 (Hebrew 9:17) employs this verb in describing divine judgment: 'Wickedness burns like a fire... it kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke.' The Hithpael form suggests reflexive or intensive action, picturing smoke spiraling upward as vegetation is consumed. The image conveys both the destructive power of judgment and its visible, ascending manifestation.

senses.1: To roll up or spiral upward, especially of smoke. Isaiah 9:18 uses this verb to describe how forest fires from God's judgment send smoke 'rolling upward' in thick columns. The reflexive verb form intensifies the image of smoke twisting and billowing skyward, making divine wrath visible and unmistakable to all observers.

gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'meadow of acacias,' designating Israel's final encampment before crossing the Jordan into Canaan. Numbers 33:49 locates the camp 'from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab.' This is the same location called simply Shittim elsewhere, where Israel committed idolatry with Moabite women and where Balaam's prophecies were delivered. The place represents both the threshold of promise and the site of serious moral failure.

senses.1: A geographical location in the plains of Moab, Israel's last camp before entering Canaan. Numbers 33:49 identifies Abel-shittim as the extent of the Israelite encampment across from Jericho. Here, on the edge of promise, Israel faced final temptation (Numbers 25) before Joshua led them across the Jordan, making it a place of both anticipation and testing.

gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'meadow of vineyards,' marking the extent of Jephthah's military campaign against the Ammonites. Judges 11:33 records that Jephthah 'struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow.' The name suggests an area known for viticulture, and its mention defines the southern limit of Jephthah's devastating victory that subdued Ammon before Israel.

senses.1: A location in Ammonite territory, the endpoint of Jephthah's campaign. Judges 11:33 names Abel-keramim ('meadow of vineyards') as the furthest extent of Jephthah's conquest, indicating a region cultivated for grapes. The geographical note emphasizes the thoroughness of Israel's victory and the wide swath of territory affected by the battle.

gloss_terse: Abel-mizraim, site near Jordan where Jacob was mourned
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'meadow of Egypt' or 'mourning of Egypt,' located beyond the Jordan where Joseph and the Egyptians mourned Jacob. Genesis 50:11 recounts that when the Canaanites saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they named it Abel-mizraim, saying 'This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.' The etymology plays on the dual meaning of 'abel'—both 'meadow' and 'mourning'—creating a wordplay that commemorates the elaborate funeral rites.

senses.1: The location where Jacob's funeral procession mourned for seven days, renamed 'mourning of Egypt.' Genesis 50:11 explains the Canaanite observers were so impressed by the Egyptian funeral rites that they named the place 'Abel-mizraim.' The name preserves the memory of extraordinary grief expressed by Joseph's Egyptian entourage for the Hebrew patriarch.

gloss_readable: The written form (Ketiv) of a river name in 2 Kings 5:12, where Naaman boasts about the rivers of Damascus. The Qere (spoken form) reads Amanah. This river, likely the Barada (ancient Chrysorrhoas), flows from the Anti-Lebanon mountains through Damascus. Naaman's rhetorical question—'Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?'—expresses his initial contempt for Elisha's instruction to wash in the Jordan.

senses.1: A river flowing through Damascus, mentioned by Naaman. 2 Kings 5:12 records Naaman's proud comparison of Damascus's rivers to Israel's Jordan. The Ketiv 'Abana' (variant: Amanah in Qere) identifies one of two famous rivers supplying Damascus with fresh water, symbols of Syrian prestige that Naaman initially values above obedience.

gloss_readable: A town in the tribal territory of Issachar, listed among the cities allotted to that tribe. Joshua 19:20 includes Ebez in the boundary description and city list for Issachar's inheritance. Little else is known about this location, and its exact site remains uncertain. Like many towns in these lists, it represents a specific land grant fulfilling God's promise to give Israel the land, even when individual sites can no longer be identified with certainty.

senses.1: A city in Issachar's tribal allotment. Joshua 19:20 names Ebez among the towns given to Issachar, fulfilling the distribution of Canaan among the twelve tribes. Though the site's exact location is lost, its inclusion in Scripture testifies to the detailed fulfillment of God's promise to give Israel specific, named territories.

gloss_terse: powders, fragrant spices ground to powder
gloss_readable: Aromatic powders, specifically the ground spices or perfumes used in cosmetic and ceremonial contexts. Song of Songs 3:6 asks, 'What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of the merchant?' The term appears in construct relationship—'powders of the merchant'—indicating imported, luxury aromatics that accompany the royal procession, creating a sensory-rich image of Solomon's approach.

senses.1: Fragrant powders or ground spices, especially imported luxury aromatics. In Song of Songs 3:6, 'the powders of the merchant' are part of the magnificent description of Solomon's wedding procession, evoking expensive perfumes that create fragrant clouds. The term emphasizes both the material (finely ground) and the commercial value (merchant's goods).

gloss_readable: To soar or fly on wings, particularly used of birds of prey. Job 39:26 asks, 'Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars and spreads its wings toward the south?' The verb, a denominative from 'wing' or 'pinion,' describes the effortless, instinctive flight of raptors as they migrate. God's rhetorical question challenges Job to recognize that such natural marvels operate by divine wisdom, not human knowledge.

senses.1: To fly or soar on wings, especially of birds of prey. Job 39:26 uses this verb in God's interrogation of Job: does the hawk soar by Job's wisdom? The question highlights the hawk's instinctive flight and migration as expressions of divine design, beyond human control or comprehension, humbling Job's attempts to question God's governance.

gloss_terse: bow the knee, proclamation of homage (uncertain)
gloss_readable: A proclamation shouted before Joseph's chariot, traditionally understood as 'Bow the knee!' though its precise meaning is uncertain. Genesis 41:43 describes Pharaoh's elevation of Joseph: 'He made him ride in his second chariot, and they called out before him,

' Scholars have proposed numerous etymologies—Egyptian, Akkadian, Hebrew—some suggesting it means 'kneel' or 'pay homage,' others 'attention' or even a title. Regardless, it clearly signals Joseph's newly exalted status.

senses.1: An acclamation of uncertain meaning proclaimed before Joseph, possibly commanding obeisance. Genesis 41:43 records this cry accompanying Joseph's public procession as vizier of Egypt. Whether the term means 'bow down,' 'make way,' or serves as an honorific title, its function is clear: announcing Joseph's authority and demanding public respect for Pharaoh's chosen administrator.

gloss_terse: Agee, father of one of David's mighty men
gloss_readable: A personal name meaning possibly 'fugitive,' identified as the father of Shammah, one of David's elite warriors. Second Samuel 23:11 introduces Shammah son of Agee the Hararite, who single-handedly defended a lentil field against the Philistines. The name appears only in this context, preserved solely because of the son's remarkable military achievement. It reminds us that many biblical names survive only through their children's deeds.

senses.1: Father of Shammah, one of David's three mighty men. 2 Samuel 23:11 identifies 'Shammah son of Agee the Hararite' among David's most heroic warriors. While we know nothing else about Agee, his name is immortalized through his son's legendary courage in defending a field of lentils against overwhelming Philistine forces.

gloss_readable: Nuts or nut trees, possibly walnuts, used collectively to refer to a nut orchard. Song of Songs 6:11 describes going 'down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vines had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.' The term likely designates walnut trees, creating a lush garden scene filled with springtime fertility and growth. The nut grove becomes a setting for romantic encounter and natural abundance.

senses.1: Nut trees or nuts, collectively describing an orchard or grove. Song of Songs 6:11 mentions 'the nut garden' as the speaker's destination to observe spring growth. This cultivated space of nut trees (likely walnuts) represents fertility, abundance, and cultivation—a fitting backdrop for the poem's exploration of love's fruitfulness.
